episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to call themselves local?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Lorne Doerkson becomes Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA and will B.C’s next premier and Author with dwarfism debuts children’s book inspired by childhood race in Horsefly, plus 12 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Who gets to decide who counts as local in Cariboo arts, culture, and storytelling, and how should written rules, records, and access be governed? Topics include: Defining local identity versus residence and publishing infrastructure in the Tommy's Race book, Transparency and membership rules in the Quesnel & District Community Arts Council, Censorship of artworks in the 1980s and 2020s and the fragility of small artist-run spaces, Federal arts funding cuts, court rulings, and digital distribution as an alternative, Heritage archives, record-keeping, and the risks of journalism under foreign-funding laws in Azerbaijan.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Quesnel & District Community Arts Council

discussion.central_question: Who gets to decide who counts as local in Cariboo arts, culture, and storytelling, and how should written rules, records, and access be governed?
discussion.riley_position: Riley argues that local claims rest on birth, childhood, and community ties, that infrastructure like publishers is part of the local story, and that written, public rules and archives make arts communities fair and resilient.
riley_key_evidence: Tommy's Race was written by someone born and raised in Horsefly, and the whole book comes from one school sports day east of Williams Lake
The Quesnel & District Community Arts Council has been an umbrella for arts, heritage, and culture since 1973, and a criteria page is an afternoon's work
Amy Sherald and Victor 'Marka27' Quiñonez saw museums move to censor their work, per Mother Jones, and digital publishing offers a second door
discussion.casey_position: Casey contends that local claims are contested and shaped by who holds money, power, and records, that unwritten gatekeeping excludes newcomers, and that cultural infrastructure and archives are fragile and can be controlled by others.
casey_key_evidence: The author lives in Kamloops, the illustrator is in Montreal, and Caitlin Press published the book, so local in subject differs from local in the paycheque
Federal courts ordered the NEH to reverse grant cancellations, but the administration appealed and no retroactive money has returned, and Artforum reports the proposed budget eliminated the NEA
Azerbaijani prosecutors requested 12-year and 11-year sentences against Imran Aliyev and Elgiz Gahraman, with CPJ reporting at least 13 journalists arrested on donor-funding allegations
discussion.resolution: They did not fully agree. Riley conceded that the binder-versus-website distinction matters and that the newcomer question is real, while Casey conceded that the publisher and courts can be real levers and that Baku and Quesnel are not directly comparable. They agreed on two checkable tests: whether membership and grant rules are readable by new artists before openings, and where the Quesnel show photographs are stored.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

These analytical threads were identified before generation. Use the findings to ground Riley's and Casey's arguments with real evidence. Develop them as substantive exchanges, not a citation list.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the Hyperallergic "War on Art Is Repeating Itself" framing supported by the current US federal arts funding fight, or is it a loose analogy to the 1980s–90s Culture Wars?

Findings: Several outlets from 2026 describe the Reagan-era fights as directly relevant to present policy. Mother Jones (July 2026) ties the NEA's history to the culture wars and notes that artists such as Amy Sherald and Victor "Marka27" Quiñonez reported museums moving to censor their work after the controversies. Revealnews reports that federal courts ordered the National Endowment for the Humanities to reverse mass grant cancellations and struck down NEA restrictions on "gender ideology," but that no retroactive NEA money was restored and the administration has appealed both rulings. Artforum's roundtable says the Trump administration's proposed budget eliminated the NEA, while a House Appropriations subcommittee proposed a 35% cut to about $135 million. American Theatre reports a proposed $29 million NEA budget with the aim of sunsetting the agency, compared with $207 million. I could not confirm the fiscal years for the Artforum and American Theatre figures from the snippets, so treat those numbers as needing a check before use on air. The Art Newspaper, citing Isaac Butler, adds a structural point: many artist-run spaces from the 1970s have closed because of reduced funding, and the work they showed was more likely to cause scandal.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue that the parallel is useful because courts and public pressure have already reversed some federal grant cancellations, and that digital distribution lets artists route around institutions that self-censor. Casey can counter that the court wins did not restore the money, that the real damage is structural (closed spaces, dependence on donors and platforms), and that "repeating itself" may hide how much smaller the surviving infrastructure is than in the 1980s. Both can use the Mapplethorpe and Franklin Furnace history as the test case for whether the analogy holds.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the CPJ report on Meclis.info hold up as a press-freedom case, and what does the prosecution actually allege?

Findings: CPJ's October 22, 2026 statement says prosecutors in Baku requested 12-year prison sentences on October 20 for Imran Aliyev, founder of Meclis.info, an independent outlet covering Azerbaijan's parliament. Caucasian Knot reports a request of 11 years for activist and data analyst Elgiz Gahraman, with the prosecutor's speech interrupted during the third defendant's case, accountant Tamella Musayeva. Aliyev has been jailed since April 2024. Amnesty's 2024 urgent action says he was charged with conspiring to bring money into the country unlawfully (Article 206.3.2 of the Criminal Code), which is the "illegal donor funding" allegation. The Institute for Human Rights reports that the case expanded in 2025 with new charges and a civil lawsuit, and that witness testimony began in July. CPJ's broader point is that authorities have arrested at least 13 journalists on similar donor-funding allegations. The government's side is that these are financial-crime charges unrelated to journalism. That is the contested point, and the source documents do not resolve it.

Suggested angle: Casey should press the strongest version of the case: the state argues it is prosecuting illegal currency and grant flows, not reporting, and a foreign-funding law is a standard tool in many countries. Riley can argue that the pattern (donor-funding charges, repeated arrests, long sentence requests) is the story, and that digital outlets are the ones at risk. This also connects to the theme: a parliament-monitoring outlet is a form of digital storytelling, and the case shows how fragile independent digital media is when it depends on foreign grants.
